name: Illusion of Control
description: People overestimate their ability to control or influence outcomes that are actually determined by chance, especially when skill-relevant cues (choice, competition, familiarity, active involvement, practice) are present even though they have no real bearing on the outcome.
design_relevance_note: Explains why letting a user 'choose their own' lottery numbers, roll a virtual die themselves, or actively participate in an otherwise-random process (loot boxes, spin-to-win wheels) increases engagement and perceived fairness even though the odds are unchanged -- a genuine ethical-risk area, not just a neutral engagement lever.
myth_risk_note: The meta-analytic effect is robust and consistently observed; no indication of a popularity/evidence mismatch.
prevalence_note: A core, frequently cited concept in gambling/gamification design ethics discourse and behavioral-economics-for-design curricula generally.

findings.description: A meta-analysis of the post-Langer experimental literature on the illusion of control found a moderate-to-large overall weighted mean effect size (D = .62, 95% CI [.49, .75]) across studies and induction factors, confirming the phenomenon is robust and consistently observed, while also finding substantial heterogeneity across studies in how the illusion is operationalized/measured — suggesting the underlying phenomenon may not be fully unitary across different dependent measures.
findings.source_title: Recent developments in the experimental investigation of the illusion of control: A meta-analytic review

findings.description: Across six studies (card games, lotteries, a novel chance game), introducing skill-relevant cues — competition, choice of ticket, familiarity of the stimulus, practice, active involvement — into objectively chance-determined tasks caused participants to express inappropriately elevated confidence in their own success probability, even though the actual outcome probability was unaffected by any of these manipulations.
findings.source_venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology

applications.title: New York City's pedestrian crosswalk buttons: most do nothing, but pressing one still feels like control
applications.description: New York City's pedestrian 'walk' buttons were largely disconnected from the traffic-signal system once the city computerized signal timing, a fact the city's own transportation officials confirmed publicly in a widely-cited 2004 New York Times report. As of a later count, only around 100 of the city's crosswalk buttons remain actually connected to the signal system, with close to 1,000 more doing nothing at all when pressed. The buttons are deliberately left in place rather than removed, because -- as psychologist Ellen Langer, whose 1975 experiments established the illusion-of-control effect, has explained -- pressing a button and directing one's attention to 'doing something' produces a genuine sense of control and reduced waiting-related stress, regardless of whether the button has any real effect on the outcome.
applications.industry_context: Municipal transportation infrastructure (New York City); the same non-functional-button pattern is separately documented for elevator door-close buttons and office thermostats.
applications.ethical_note: This is intentional deception by a public authority: pedestrians are led to believe their action controls the signal when, for the large majority of these buttons, it does not. The psychological benefit is real and genuine per Langer's own research -- reduced frustration and a real sense of agency while waiting -- and no one is materially worse off for pressing a button that does nothing. Still graded mixed rather than user_beneficial, because deceiving the public about how a civic system actually works carries its own real cost to institutional trust, independent of whether the immediate individual effect is benign.
